title: Change Freeze Override Approval Lost Between Slack Workspaces
question: For the postmortem, was the deploy of PR-4892 a valid change freeze exception per Meridian's documented change management policy?
choices: A) No — the exception was never valid because it lacked a Jira Change Request ticket and was not posted in #change-management, regardless of Divya's informal approval
B) Yes — Marco communicated the exception in #engineering which constitutes a written channel notification; the only violation was the shortened canary window
C) Yes — VP Engineering (Divya) gave explicit approval via DM, which constitutes written authorization; the deploy was valid but the canary duration was the root policy violation
D) No — the exception expired because Divya's approval was given on May 12 for 'tonight' but the deploy happened on May 14, making the approval stale
rationale: Per Confluence Change Management Policy v3.1, Section 4.2, change freeze exceptions require (1) written approval from VP Eng or above, (2) documented in the #change-management channel, AND (3) a linked Jira Change Request ticket. The deploy fails on criteria 2 and 3: Marco posted in #engineering on the legacy workspace (not #change-management), and no Jira CR ticket exists. Divya's DM constitutes informal approval only — the policy explicitly states 'verbal or informal approvals are not valid per SOC2 control CC-7.2.' Answer C incorrectly treats a Slack DM as valid written authorization under SOC2 controls. Answer C confuses #engineering (legacy workspace) with the required #change-management channel and ignores the missing Jira ticket. Answer D invents a temporal expiration issue — the timeline from May 12 DM to May 13 communication to May 14 deploy is actually coherent ('tonight' referred to the night of May 13-14), but the deploy is invalid regardless due to the missing formal artifacts.

title: Conflicting Postmortem Action Items from Sequential Incidents
scenario:
**Jira — SRE-2201 'Postmortem Action: Increase circuit breaker timeout to 10s' (Created: Mar 8, 2026)**
Type: Postmortem Action Item | Priority: P1 | Status: Done (completed Mar 22)
Linked incident: INC-4302 (cascading failure in order-service due to downstream timeout at 3s causing retry storms)
Postmortem conclusion: '3s timeout was too aggressive for payment-gateway calls during peak load. Increase to 10s to prevent premature circuit-breaking.'
Assignee: @alex.martinez | Reviewer: @jordan.kim
Comment (@jordan.kim, Mar 22): 'Deployed to prod. SLIs look stable. Closing.'

**Jira — SRE-2287 'Postmortem Action: Reduce circuit breaker timeout to 5s' (Created: Apr 19, 2026)**
Type: Postmortem Action Item | Priority: P1 | Status: Open
Linked incident: INC-4389 (single-tenant degradation caused 10s hang times propagating to shared services, violating SLO)
Postmortem conclusion: 'The 10s timeout allowed a degraded downstream to hold connections too long, exhausting the connection pool. Reduce to 5s maximum with adaptive backoff.'
Assignee: @priya.singh | Reviewer: @jordan.kim
Comment (@priya.singh, Apr 22): 'This contradicts SRE-2201. Which wins?'
Comment (@jordan.kim, Apr 22): 'Good catch. Let me get context from the March incident owners.'
[No further comments]

**Confluence — 'Circuit Breaker Standards' (Page version 4, last edited Mar 24, 2026)**
Section 2.1: Default circuit breaker timeout for inter-service calls: 10s (updated per INC-4302 postmortem).
Section 2.3: Services classified as 'shared-critical' must not hold connections longer than SLO budget allows.
[RESOLVED COMMENT by @nadia.okonkwo, Apr 20]: 'This 10s default directly caused INC-4389. We need tiered timeouts: 10s for dedicated downstreams, 5s max for shared-critical. Tagging @jordan.kim'
[Comment was resolved by @nadia.okonkwo on Apr 21 with no reply from Jordan]

**Slack — #sre-team (Apr 23, 2026, 9:14 AM)**
@priya.singh: @jordan.kim did you see Nadia's comment on the circuit breaker doc? She resolved it herself but the suggestion makes sense — tiered approach.
@jordan.kim: Yeah I think that's right. Shared-critical gets 5s, everything else stays at 10s.
@priya.singh: Should I update the Confluence page or wait for the formal review?
@jordan.kim: Just update it. We'll ratify in next week's SRE sync.
[No Confluence edit was made as of May 1]

**PagerDuty — On-call rotation for order-service (current)**
Primary: @priya.singh | Secondary: @alex.martinez
Runbook link: points to Confluence 'Circuit Breaker Standards' (version 4 — still shows 10s flat default)

**Datadog — SLO Dashboard (as of May 1, 2026)**
order-service 30-day SLO: 99.91% (budget remaining: 12%)
payment-gateway p99: 4.2s (within 5s threshold but approaching)
question: It is May 1. Priya is on-call and order-service begins showing elevated latency against payment-gateway (a shared-critical service). Per Meridian's current authoritative configuration, what circuit breaker timeout is in effect for this call path?
choices: A) 5s — SRE-2287 (the more recent postmortem action item) supersedes SRE-2201 per Meridian's 'latest postmortem wins' convention
B) 10s — the Confluence page (version 4) is the runbook-linked authoritative source and it still specifies 10s flat default
C) 3s — SRE-2287 is still Open/unimplemented, meaning the pre-SRE-2201 configuration (3s) is what's actually deployed
D) 5s — Jordan approved the tiered approach in Slack, making shared-critical services subject to the 5s maximum
rationale: The authoritative source is what is actually deployed and documented. SRE-2201 was completed (status: Done) on March 22, setting the timeout to 10s. This was reflected in Confluence version 4 (edited Mar 24). SRE-2287, which calls for 5s, is still in 'Open' status — it was never implemented. Jordan's Slack message agreeing to the tiered approach was informal direction that was never acted upon (no Confluence edit was made, no deploy occurred). The on-call runbook points to Confluence v4 which states 10s. Answer A confuses a Slack conversation about intent with an actual configuration change — the Confluence page was never updated. Answer C invents a 'latest postmortem wins' rule that doesn't exist; postmortem action items only take effect when completed. Answer D incorrectly assumes that because SRE-2287 is open, the change from SRE-2201 was also reverted — but SRE-2201 is Done and its 10s change is in production.

question: In the INC-4512 postmortem, was the escalation path that PagerDuty followed on May 9 correct according to the current authoritative escalation policy?
choices: A) Partially — the escalation path was correct but the timing was wrong; Level 2 should have had a 10-minute timeout but only waited 5 minutes before escalating to Level 3
B) Yes — PagerDuty is the system of record for escalation routing, the policy was updated May 5, and the system correctly escalated Primary -> Secondary -> SRE Manager
C) No — the Confluence runbook is the authoritative escalation reference and it specifies EM at Level 2, which PagerDuty skipped
D) No — Nadia's policy change was never formally approved; the Slack thumbsup reactions do not constitute a valid change approval per Meridian's change management policy
rationale: Jordan explicitly states in the DM that 'PD is the system of record for escalation routing.' The PagerDuty policy was updated on May 5, 2026, and the incident occurred on May 9. The new policy (Primary -> Secondary -> SRE Manager -> VP Eng) was correctly followed: Priya (L1, no ack at 5 min) -> Alex (L2, no ack at 10 min) -> Nadia (L3, ack at 02:31). The timeline math confirms correct timeout intervals (02:14 + 5min = 02:19 escalation, 02:19 + 10min = 02:29 escalation). Answer A incorrectly treats the stale Confluence runbook as authoritative over the live PagerDuty configuration — this is a common failure where humans trust documentation over the actual system state. Answer C applies change management policy (which governs code deploys and infrastructure changes) to an operational tool configuration update — escalation policy changes don't require the same formal CR process. Answer D is factually wrong on the math: L2 escalated at 02:29, which is exactly 10 minutes after the 02:19 L2 page, matching the configured timeout.
